utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, we had to interrupt your submission last night because of time. Is there more that you would like to put?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With regard to the submission, I just wish to reply to that briefly and then my cross-examination should take no more than 30 minutes. That's what I'm hoping, but sometimes the witness answers in a long way. May I just deal with the submission? I wish to put --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's where I was expecting you to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just dealing with, just dealing with the matters I would like to put to the witness, we submit it goes to his credibility. There are matters that we would suggest indicate that he may have been responsible for the shelling of the town of Gorazde. We would submit that we have a document here, signed by him, indicating that they opened artillery fire at the enemy positions and the town of Gorazde. We would submit that is an issue that goes to his credibility. He can either accept it or deny it and we move on. It is something the Court can evaluate. My learned friend is only partially correct when he submitted yesterday that it was not at my witness that this matter had been clarified by earlier submissions. If my memory serves me correctly, part of the cross-examination and significant cross-examination by my learned friends of Dr. Bosanac, and I think at least one other, was that they had various allegations that they were facing in Serbia, and that was done obviously to impeach their credibility. We would submit it's exactly the same test. It is not a matter that will take any length of time, it may well be the witness does not accept it is him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic in particular, I think, referred to your objection to cross-examination of the witness Agotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't know if it was Mr. Lukic who submitted it. Agotic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that was over the nature of certain helicopter flights two years or one year after these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm trying to, trying to remember because there have been so many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May I pass you the transcript and the ruling that was against Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I imagine Mr. Lukic would remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the problem is, it's somewhat possibly to be seen as on all fours with the present position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Of course it does apply. One also has to bear in mind the -- yes, it's not me. I thought it wasn't me. It is Mr. Agotic -- so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Oh, well you can shed responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I must say I was getting extremely worried. I thought, I'm really in trouble here. So I feel much better, personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Then as legal counsel you are on top of everything happening in the case, aren't you? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But all I would submit -- yes. No, I wouldn't want that. But all I'm submitting is, when one looks at the cross-examination of Dr. Bosanac, there were significant documents brought out alleging the fact that she had breached various matters and was consequently being impeached. And it could have been for no other reason, her credibility. That, I would submit, is the appropriate test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were those matters not contemporaneous or approximately so with the events in issue in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: They would have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And in the same location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: They would have been, of course; I accept that entirely. But may I equally submit the following. If one looks to -- and I will submit by way of analogy for national jurisdiction -- if a person facing a trial, let us say in 19 -- for acts committed in 1991, and he is -- there is significant material by his own hand to demonstrate that he may well have been responsible for the commission of a criminal act. Subsequently, is the Court seriously suggesting -- and I don't mean that offencively -- that that is not evidence that can be taken into account? It's not a question of me just putting it to him. I have a document, signed by this man, in relation to that matter. So it's not a case of the challenge, per se. It is a question of the document which he is the author of and, therefore, in a position to deal with. And therefore we would submit there is a distinction. That would be my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I think that the position here is the same that I put forward yesterday with regard to witness Imra Agotic. And when the issue of the participation of a witness was raised, I believe it was Vilim Karlovic in the Storm Operation, storm and lightning. And when the position was also taken that the questioning of that witness with regard to his credibility and the circumstances from subsequent years was not admissible with regard to this case and this indictment. The comparison to what we asked Ms. Vesna Bosanac, we agree with you that she was exclusively questioned with regard to this indictment and the events at that time. I believe that the position of the Court was that this was no way to question the credibility of the witness in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you've had your intervention, Mr. Lukic. That's it. Thank you. You are not directly the party calling the witness or cross-examining, you see, but -- we hear you once, but there are limits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is the view of the Chamber that the cross-examination, pursuing what apparently is alleged conduct in a different unit, although involving the witness something like two years after the event in a different venue entirely is not something that is going to assist the Tribunal in the resolution of this case. Credibility is advanced as the basis for the cross-examination and credibility, of course, is always in issue in every case involving every witness. We have to consider whether an issue, which has no apparent link with the events we're dealing with is one which is likely to have an effect upon our assessment of the credibility of that witness in this case. As we have ruled in an earlier matter concerning the witness, Agotic, evidence which is so long after the event and so removed physically and -- in terms of the military units involved from the issues in this case. Although it may give rise to the possibility of some improper conduct by the witness is so removed that we are not in a position that we could anticipate that their appreciation of the credibility of the witness, for the purposes of this trial, would be affected in any material way. So for those reasons, Mr. Moore, the cross-examination on that issue should not be pursued. If we could now have the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there is a medical update. It may well be that Your Honour would wish to deal with that. And secondly, as Your Honour knows, there will be some legal argument. After we conclude with the witness of Danilovic, I think there are no other witnesses. So I don't know if Your Honour was thinking of taking a break between the legal arguments and the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We were going to see first when you and Mr. Vasic finished with the witness, and then assess whether we had any time left, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would remind you that the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Danilovic, I have very few questions for you. So could you just keep your answers short and we can finish the matter quickly. I want to deal with the officers that you served. I want to -- you told us about one of your officers that you served with. I would like to deal with Mr. Vukosavljevic in charge of the security organ for the 80th. Would it be right to say that you knew him at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How would you describe Mr. Vukosavljevic as an officer?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that Mr. Vukosavljevic was a good officer. He was a reserve officer. He had graduated from the school for reserve officers, and even though I'm not acquainted with the details of the work of the security organ, but I think that he was good at performing his duty in accordance with his training as a reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And would you agree that he is not only an officer but a man of integrity?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that he, as a person, is honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You're not suggesting presumably he's dishonest. You're just saying you can say?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I answered your question, Mr. Moore. He was responsible. He was conscientious. I never noticed him doing anything dishonest. During the time we spent together at the time of the 80th Motorised Brigade, that is the time I'm referring to. We didn't know each other before that, nor did we socialise privately, so I don't know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I understand now your reservations. But your dealing with him, as far as you could see he was professional, competent, and did his work well. That would be the analysis, would it not?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he worked well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With regard to Mr. Vezmarovic, he had an extremely responsible job on the night of the 18th and morning of the 19th, that is correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Moore. Since -- the company of the military police that he commanded was charged with providing security for the prisoners of war, so his task was doubtlessly responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And as far as you could see, he did that task well and responsibly?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he did -- he performed his task at the time responsibly and well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we deal, please, with Miodrag Panic. Now, Miodrag Panic as you are well aware was the Chief of Staff of OG South, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you know Miodrag Panic before he went to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. You will have the information that we graduated from military academy together and that we had known each other for at least two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sir, when did you graduate?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I graduated from military academy on July 30th, 1972, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you have known Miodrag Panic since 1972, is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I can only speak about graduation in an English army, but when you're officer or junior officers in an English army you tend to keep your friendships from people that you have served with from different units. Does that apply -- did that apply to the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well to be completely frank, I can confirm that it was the case in my army too. We were friends and if we meet each other again, especially on combat duties, we would support each other and cooperate well. That's the truth. There is no escaping from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dealing with Miodrag Panic. Clearly you served together in Vukovar. After you or they, the OG South of the guards, left Vukovar, did you serve again together?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Moore. We did not share any duty. Only I remember we once inspected the combat readiness of the military district in Kragujevac where I was commander for some four and a half years. As far as I remember, that was in 2002 or 2001, around that time. I didn't expect a question like this, so it isn't readily, this information isn't readily accessible in my memory, so I'm not sure about the period. I remember it was in March, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just would you allow me one moment. When was the last time you saw Miodrag Panic?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will trust me when I give you my word as an officer, we never saw each other again after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you've had no dealings with him then in the organisation of the Defence of Mr. Mrksic? He didn't contact you?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Moore, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever make a statement to the lawyers dealing with Mr. Mrksic's Defence about the evidence you would give?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I did. It would have been in December or January, this year, if I'm not mistaken, when I talked to the lawyers about the Defence. I was told at the time that three officers from the Guards Brigade, General Mrksic, Colonel Sljivancanin, and Captain Radic, the -- but the concrete questions, they said that this -- they would be about that grave incident at Ovcara. I didn't understand that to mean that I would be part of the Defence of General Mrksic, but I was ready to say that, since they are really honourable officers. I don't know whether you know, but only the best officers were appointed to guard units. The best officers of the then JNA. That's what I can say, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well then can you just assist me, are you saying -- or perhaps a better way of putting it is this. When is the first time you were aware of the allegations of atrocities at Ovcara, which was within the zone of responsibility of your regiment?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Moore. That was the zone of responsibility of the brigade, is all my remark. I found out about that and -- in former contacts with soldiers and officers of the 80th Motorised Brigade, but it was said that those atrocities had been committed by the TO -- by members of TO Vukovar, without the mention of any particular individuals. I cannot say that they were really those who committed it, but I didn't deal with this issue any further because I had many other tasks, as Chief of Staff of the 80th Motorised Brigade. And this, I didn't want to burden myself with this work, with this issue, because it didn't seem to me that members of the 80th Motorised Brigade were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sir, when did you cease being Chief of Staff of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I think that I remained in that position officially until June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you told us that you were told by soldiers and officers of the 80th, clearly within your tenure of Chief of Staff of the 80th Motorised Brigade, so I'm asking you when.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was after my return from my assignment in the village of Nemci, and later Tovarnik where I inspected the 2nd Motorised Battalion, which then suffered many losses and there were problems with the morale. So upon my return to the command, on those days I heard, and in former conversations with some soldiers and officers, that this incident had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So it was when you returned on the 21st?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 21st or 22nd, around in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what were you hearing was being said?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I heard that members of TO Vukovar had massacred the captured members of the ZNG and the MUP of the Republic of Croatia. There were some conjectures about the number of people killed, but I do not remember exactly what the figures were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it was in relation to the location, it was around Ovcara; within the zone of responsibility, unfortunately, of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately that is the case, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So what did you ask Colonel Mrksic, when you found out about that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not entertain any official or unofficial contacts with Mr. Mrksic and I'm sure he can confirm that for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't want to involve ourselves with Mr. Mrksic. I just want to deal with you. I'm not trying to blame. I'm just trying to find out. Do you understand? Here was a situation: You find out that atrocities have been committed by TO Vukovar within the zone of responsibility of the 80th Motorised Brigade. You are the Chief of Staff of the 80th Motorised Brigade. That is a position of significant responsibility. Who did you speak to? What officers did you speak to, to tell them about the information that you had received, either by way of unofficial or informal conversation or by way of document?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, since I was involved in this mission, and I've given you detailed account of that, when I returned, at the brigades there was the brigade commander as well as all the other officers. I had heard informally about this regrettable incident, and I simply believed that the brigade commander would be taking all the appropriate steps, because he was the one actually present at the command post. I definitely did not feel that I was the person responsible for taking any measures. That was my take on the situation, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like you please to look at Exhibit 396. Before it's put on the screen, and it's my fault, I would just ask one or two other questions. Are you saying that you did or you did not speak to any superior officer about this information?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I did not. But this was all a long time ago and you can hardly expect me to be entirely positive about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I suggest to you that a person can expect you to be entirely positive about that, unless, of course, you're a person who is aware of a number of atrocities and you forget which ones we're dealing with, Atrocities do not tend to arise in most peoples lives, Mr. Danilovic. Do you understand? So I would suggest you can remember. So can I take it that you did not consult a senior officer?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Feel free to assume that, Mr. Moore. As for any senior officers, from the level of the 80th Motorised Brigade up, I certainly did not share that with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like to then to refer you to the 1988 "Regulations of the Application of the International Laws of War." Paragraph 21, please. Now, I have 19 and 20. I'm going to have to go through it on 19 and 20. What do you have in front of you? What is shown on the screen?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see is measures to prevent violations of the law of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just want to check to see what's being shown. We've got them all. So let's just go through it. 19 relates to the responsibility of the parties to a conflict for violations of the laws of war. The parties to a conflict shall be responsible for violations of the laws of war. Regardless of whether the violations occurred following the orders of, or with the knowledge of the governments or supreme commands or whether they resulted from the willful actions of members of their armed forces, other organs and individuals acting as representatives of organs. So just looking at number 19, article 19, you accept that as an officer you were informed, on the 21 or 22nd of atrocities in the Ovcara area by the Vukovar TO. That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, it is not quite the way you put it. I can only repeat that whenever I talk to soldiers and officers from the command and our subordinate units informally, it was said every time that some of the captured ZNG and MUP members had been killed by the TO men. I did not even know that this was the other group of prisoners who had been brought over from the hospital. I didn't even know that the whole thing was about those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Forgive me for being a little cynical. But here you are, you come back from a tour to Nemci. You come back and you're informed by officers and soldiers of your brigade that Vukovar TO have murdered people in your zone of responsibility. Are you saying you didn't ask how this happened? Or who they were? Is that what you're actually expecting not only this Court, but the world to believe?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, I'm telling it like it was. I'm telling you about what I knew. I can hardly tell you anything other than what I knew. Again, I didn't really ask around, the reason being the people involved were TO men. And they committed this execrable atrocity. Secondly, I was not physically present at the command to be able to know about this directly. Thirdly, I thought the commanders and the assistant commanders were there. They were sufficiently able to take any measures that were necessary, about this or about anything else. That's why I'm telling you what I'm telling you. This is simply how it happened, and there is precious little that I can do to change that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I respectfully submit to you and suggest to you, you're talking complete nonsense. That in actual fact you were aware that the Vukovar TO were subordinated to OG South.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, it is not my intention to offend you. But you should be an honourable judge too. I'm sorry to have to say this. You have just suggested I'm talking nonsense. Well, we might as well just let that be. But the Vukovar TO Staff was not subordinated to the command of OG South [as interpreted]. This is clearly indicated by a number of documents. If you allow me some time I could track them down for you. We only worked with the TO Staff, but it didn't go any further than that, and that is a fact, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm afraid the fact is that we have had a large amount of evidence and, indeed, it is accepted by your Defence counsel on the other side, that the Vukovar TO were subordinated to OG South. So when you look to your left and you see all the lawyers who are operating on the basis of the instructions of their counsel, of their defendants, they accept the Vukovar TO were subordinated to OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. I think there is an error in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and that is what has caused all of this confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's about an error in the transcript. The witness said that the Vukovar TO was not subordinated to the command of OG South. That is page 14, lines 25 and then line 1. That's what the witness said, but the transcript suggests that the Vukovar TO were subordinated -- the staff. I'm talking about the TO Staff. So the witness never said anything about OG South. He referred to the command of the 80th Brigade. I think that is what brought about all of this confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which line do you say is in error?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the page is 14, line 25, and page 15, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My version of it says the Vukovar TO Staff were not subordinated to OG South. Is that not what the witness said?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said the TO Staff was not subordinated to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade. So there is the error. Your Honours, with all due respect, it says subordinated to OG South, whereas the witness said the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So it's the unit to which they were subordinated that is the error?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We will attempt to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: TO Vukovar, forget about TO Vukovar staff. TO Vukovar, you knew because you'd been there for a long time, were subordinated to OG South. That is something that is accepted by everyone in this Court.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that the Vukovar TO Staff was not subordinated to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade. I'm sorry. But I can't really tell you about anything else. I'm just not positive. I don't know for sure. But I don't challenge that, Mr. Moore. Mind you, I don't challenge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have the staff. You have the units. Do you agree with that, subdivision for the moment, militarily?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We take away the staff, and I'm saying the TO Vukovar units were subordinated to OG South. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been logical for the TO units to be subordinated to the Vukovar TO Staff according to our military logic. Now, some of the TO staff units may have been subordinated to the command of OG South, but this is hardly the kind of information that you can expect from me. I simply didn't know. I wasn't privy to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Oh, I would suggest you most certainly were privy to it. You were a Chief of Staff. This is an entirely -- a very unique position. Chief of Staff is really the eyes and ears of his commander. He is in a position to take up the reins if anything should happen. So this is not some sort of company commander. You were in a very, very specific position. I would suggest you know perfectly well that TO Vukovar was subordinated to OG South. But you just don't want to admit it, same way you didn't want to admit that in actual fact Mr. Mrksic would have been responsible in the line of command if he'd been told by Vojnovic about the atrocities. Exactly the same position. You don't want to admit any guilt at all.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I really want us to stay on respectful terms. I'm telling you that the Vukovar TO Staff was not subordinated to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade. Likewise, I'm telling you, and I'm sure you can verify that, that the TO Staff units were under the command of the same TO Vukovar staff. As for this other thing that you're trying to get me to say, and that I know nothing about, that the TO Staff was subordinated to OG South, or rather, that units belonging to that staff were subordinated to OG South, I simply do not know and don't expect me to say it. I have to be open about this. I'm somewhat offended by this. Because the way you seem to be approaching this is mistrustfully, as if I were telling you something that was false. And you know, as well as I do, that I have taken an oath to tell the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Let's forget about being soldiers. Let's just be human beings. I'm not saying they can't be the same thing, but let's just try being human beings today. Here you are. You come back and you find out, from your officers and your soldiers, that atrocities, murders, have been killed in the zone of responsibility of your unit. Now, didn't that concern you, as just a human being?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, again, there was no official meeting at the command about this. The brigade commander said nothing to me about this. Nor did he instruct me to take any steps or measures about this. Given the fact that word did get around informally among soldiers and officers that this had been done by Vukovar's TO men, and with the competing pressures of great losses and a lot of other problems in the brigade, I simply didn't dedicate myself this problem in the belief that the brigade commander would be taking all the appropriate steps, because during this most regrettable event he was the commanding officer present at the command. You are certainly free to misconstrue the whole thing as being my responsibility. I can only leave you to it, and I believe the Chamber will be judging everybody's responsibility, including mine, that goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But it's right what you say that Vojnovic never mentioned it to you?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: We simply didn't discuss that, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, no, no?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You said Vojnovic never mentioned it to you. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic did not talk to me about that. He did not discuss that with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well then how do you know that Mr. Vojnovic was unaware of what had happened? He mightn't have, mightn't have said anything to you because he didn't know. And therefore, wasn't it beholden on you to check whether in actual fact: Commander, I have heard rumours, more than rumours that there were atrocities in our zone of responsibility. So he mightn't have known. Not a case of him hiding. So what did you actually do about it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: About this event? I'm not sure that I was clear enough. I didn't do anything, in the belief that the brigade commander was at the command post and I was elsewhere, on a different mission, in the belief, as I said, that the brigade commander would be taking all the relevant steps that needed taking. Did the commander know at the time? Did he not? It's not something that I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ask him?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, Mr. Moore. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not going to deal with this point much more. I would suggest that you, as a Chief of Staff and in a position of responsibility, had a duty either to ask your commanding officer about it, ask the security organ about it, or put something in place to ensure that enquiries, at the very least, should be made. And I would suggest that you are deliberately evading the truth in this Court because you will not own up to your responsibilities. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I am simply astonished by what you are putting to me, to be brutally frank. It was my desire to appeal -- to appear in this courtroom and tell you what I know about what happened. Now you're shifting the blame to me. You have every right to. You are, after all, a Prosecutor. But what I can tell you, with sure and certain knowledge, is that none of my officers from the staff command ordered or committed that crime. The commander was at the command post. If there were any steps that needed taking, I believe that he would make sure the steps were taken, or else he would have ordered me to take measures in addition to my regular assignments and tasks at the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like you to look at paragraph 21, please, of the "Basic Provisions of Prevention of Violations of the International Laws of War." Have you got it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you see the title, "Responsibility for the Actions of Subordinates"?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What does this section encompass? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please have some time to go through it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are trying to hurry me along here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am not trying to hurry you along. You can read it.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just indicate, I am not saying to you that TO Vukovar was subordinated to the 80th Motorised Brigade. Do you understand? I am not suggesting that.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well you can't possibly be suggesting that because he was not subordinated and that's clear on the face of the documents that we have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am not suggesting it. What I am suggesting, however, is that TO Vukovar had to be subordinated to someone. That is correct, isn't it? It wasn't the 80th, but they were subordinated to someone.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can do is make assumptions, but I can't tell you who they were subordinated to, I really can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will ask you the question one more time. TO Vukovar was subordinated to someone; that is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to be subordinated to someone, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Exactly. Now let's look at this particular issue. Here you are, Chief of Staff of the 80th Motorised Brigade. We use the word "atrocities." Let's use the word "murders," a large number of murders occurring on your zone of responsibility. I would suggest you would want to know who on earth was the officer, or who on earth was this unit subordinated to. That's just a normal human reaction. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, I think I've said a lot of things. If you take my answers, you should be able to glean what the conclusion is about this event. You keep pressing the point. You keep saying that I was supposed to do something about this or about that. Take measures. Take steps. And I can responsibly claim that at a difficult time like that, with the brigade facing so much hardship, so many different problems, I firmly believe that the brigade commander and the brigade's officers, all of the brigade's officers, I'm saying, if indeed this had occurred, because I never took this up with my commander, nor was there a meeting about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- if I may just be allowed to finish my answer. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm asking you a specific question. I'm not asking about others. I'm asking about you. Please deal with you and you alone. You're a Chief of Staff. You have murders happening on your zone of responsibility by a military unit who is subordinated to someone. I would suggest it is logical and sensible to ask: Who on earth is this unit subordinated to? Are you saying you did not ask that question of yourself?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- I didn't ask myself. That's how it was. Maybe it's not the answer you want, but the truth of the matter is, I didn't ask myself. And I've given you all the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And TO Vukovar, by name, was operating within the zone of responsibility of OG South. You knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was also operating within the zone of responsibility of the 80th Brigade. It's all true. No question about it. We would all have been much better off if they had been operating in accordance with the law of war, but we see that acts of madness were committed too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And therefore operating within the zone of OG South meant that Mrksic should have been approached about this issue. Because he is the senior officer to whom these units are subordinated. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I cannot confirm whether or not the units of TO Vukovar were subordinated to OG South. You are now, again, making me or trying to make me say that. I really don't know that. I would really ask you not to insist on this part, not to press this point. There must be witnesses who can tell you more about that. I do not have any further information about this and I cannot say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Tell me. Did you say you're an honest witness? That actually you have come to tell the truth? Is what you've been saying the truth and we should apply the standard, the replies that you have given here, to all of your evidence? Is that what you're saying? This Court can rely on you?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, I believe that is absolutely the case. I've told you all I knew about these events from the time when I was Chief of Staff. If you doubt my sincerity, that must -- you must have your reasons. But I can only tell this Chamber that this is really the way it was. If you are claiming the opposite, then, please, show that to me based on a written document. We're talking about a time that was 15 years ago, and remembering everything is very difficult. I believe you will agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I hope I'll be forgiven the following. It is not a case of doubting your sincerity. It is a case of doubting your honesty. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will choose a different vocabulary now than my learned friend. Good morning, Mr. Danilovic.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do reorganise your stuff. I won't interrupt you. I will go back to some questions and answers that you gave to my learned friends yesterday and today in order to clarify some things in the re-examination. Please stick to the same tempo as in the examination-in-chief. Please wait a little while after my question and then start your answer.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Upon -- rather, to the question of my learned friend, Mr. Lukic, you spoke about your duties as commander of the security element in the detention camp in the night of 18 to 19th of November, and then you said that when the group was taken to Sremska Mitrovica from your camp, that part of the task of the 80th Brigade was accomplished. I would like to know what the second part of the task was, if the transfer of this group was only one part.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant that the first part -- when I said -- I meant that the first part was the transfer of this group of prisoners of war, and the second part would have been the evacuation of those captured around the hospital in Vukovar. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Asked by my learned friend, Mr. Lukic, you also spoke about the relations that were in place on the 18th of November, 1991 -- or rather communications to the hangar of the -- between the hangar and the 80th Brigade. And you were also asked about the communication between LAD PVO and the command of the 80th Brigade. So let's clarify this. Do you know what the communication was like between the LAD PVO and the command of the 80th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I know for certain that there was radio communication in place between the brigade command and the immediately subordinated units. There was also - there was also a wire link to them. I don't remember every detail, but I know that there was communication between the brigade command at Negoslavci and Ovcara, where the provision of the POW camp was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what kind of communication was in place on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was radio communication. There wasn't enough time to establish a wire link, but I cannot tell you for sure because it was a long time ago, I must tell you frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now refer to the part of the questioning by my learned friend, Mr. Moore. I would first refer to what Mr. Moore showed you and asked you to find in the operations log, entry of order, the entry of the order sent by the command of military district -- the military district, which is under number 450. Could you please take a look at the operations log, which is Exhibit 371. You may remember that yesterday and the day before we discussed a number of orders here that concern the resubordination, the establishment of the -- this town command, et cetera. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Then now I will ask you to focus on the following numbers, which I would like you to look up in the operations log. Command of OG South, strictly confidential, 405-1, which is Exhibit 412. This is about the resubordination order.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I take a pen to take notes, because it will be difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Please look at the following order first, the -- from the command of OG South, strictly confidential, 405-1, dated 15th of November, 1991, which is Exhibit 412. The second document -- I will now give you the data for a number of documents. So the second document is the order of the command of OG South, strictly confidential, 446-1, dated 20th of November, 1991. Exhibit 425. Then please have a look at the order of the command of the first motorised district, strictly confidential, 2436-1, dated 20th of November, 1991, which is Exhibit 7 -- Exhibit 778. Then please make a note of the following, the order of the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade, number 29/2, dated 16th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: 29, slash what?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Slash 2. Strictly confidential, dated 16th of November, which is Exhibit 776. Just a moment. The order of the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade, 34-2, dated 22nd of November, 1991. So I have now made an arbitrary selection of orders that are admitted into evidence. So please take -- have a look at order 15-22. Is any of these orders entered in the operations log and were those orders entered into -- in the operations log in November 1991, in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say right away that these orders mostly were not entered in the operations log, which I can verify now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, do check first.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for what reason, but, all right, yes, I will check. Mr. Vasic, I wasn't able to find any of these orders in the operations log. I believe I haven't skipped anything. You will have followed it too, but I simply couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I think that all of us here in this courtroom, who had a chance to look at the operations log, will agree that these -- the orders under these numbers I gave are not there, but this is an issue of the evaluation of evidence. Let's continue. My colleague asked you about the order of the command of the military district which is Exhibit 415, can I have that on the screen, please. It's an order of the command of the first motorised district dated November 18th, 1991. This was discussed both in the examination-in-chief and in the cross-examination. And it includes an item about atrocities committed by some TO members and the warning to take care that such crimes are not committed. Do you remember Mr. Moore talking to you about that?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he did insist that I give him an answer about this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you, and you answered that you did not have this order of the 1st Military District in your hands. The Prosecutor also asked you whether you would have -- you would remember if such an order had been sent to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade, mentioning murders committed by the TO, and you answered that you would remember. Let me ask you. What would have been your answer if Mr. Moore had asked you whether you had the order of the commander of OG South in your hands, which was issued based on the order given by the command of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there was such an order. I would like to see it, though, because I have difficulty remembering. I really do not remember this order. But I think an order of OG South should have arrived at the brigade command and, based on that, we forwarded orders to immediately subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But unfortunately we were unable to lay hands on some orders and logs, just as the log of the 1st Guard Brigade, so we have to rely on the memory of our witnesses. Let us continue. Let us get back to the hangar at Ovcara, to the 18th of November, 1991, when you were commander of that hangar. And then you discussed with my learned friend whether the prisoners of war kept there were fearful or not. You also said -- you stated your opinion, why they would have been fearful. But I will ask you about something else. While they were entering the hangar, did security have their weapons pointed at them?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic, I believe that Mr. Moore also understood me saying that the barrels of automatic rifles were pointed at -- were pointed at the prisoners of war, to prevent them from trying to escape, or doing anything else stupid. I didn't really comment on that, but that was one of the elements that could have given rise to fear. Let me not go into other things that may have been on their minds at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would like to know, now, were these rifles pointed at them all the time until they were taken to Sremska Mitrovica from the hangar?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Weapons were ready to be used all the time, lest they should try to escape or do anything else. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I now see Exhibit 256, photograph 22. Could we please zoom in on the portion where the hangars can be seen. Mr. Danilovic, do you recognise these buildings?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you identify the building in which the POW camp was set up on the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is the one near the front side.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could the Usher please hand the witness the magic pen, as we call it. Sir, could you please put a number "1" to mark the hangar in which the POWs were held on the 18th of November. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's the one. Although the last time I laid eyes on it was on the 18th of November, 1991, but I think that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Evidence provided by the witnesses seems to corroborate what you are saying. Do you perhaps remember in which part of the hangar the prisoners were held?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, they were at this end of the hangar. Looking from this side, it's an aerial view, the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you're pointing out the left-hand side, the right-hand side is the other side, isn't it? You're saying "right" and you are pointing left, aren't you? Look here, there are two doors. There is one on the right-hand side and one on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. It was at this end. I was somewhat confused by the road leading to the hangar. That's what caused me to lose my bearings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were saying the right thing yet pointing at the wrong thing, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. This is the part that I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please put a number 2 there.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please save this photograph and I move that it be admitted into evidence as marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 782, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We'll no longer be requiring the magic pen. Thank you very much. Can we please have Exhibit 371 pulled up now. That's the operations log of the 80th Motorised Brigade. The entry we need is the one in relation to the 18th of November, 1600 hours. The witness has a hard copy in B/C/S available; therefore, we can pull the English up and, in the English, this is page, page 8. We've got that on our monitors. Thank you. Mr. Danilovic, can we look at the 1600 hours entry. It says: "The first group with around 70 Ustasha was taken by trucks to detention for the night. Another hundred of them were brought over, Lieutenant Colonel Rade Danilovic was appointed commander." Where it says another 100 of them were brought over, was that later on in the course of the night or earlier on?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't pinpoint the time when this other group arrived, Mr. Vasic. My assumption is this might have occurred in the first part of the night, earlier on. But the prisoners themselves might be better able to tell you, fortunately those survived and they might be able to say. As for me, I really can't pinpoint the exact time for you right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Danilovic. However, you are certain that this was during that night, right?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that much is certain. There's no question about that. It couldn't have been during the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The way I see this entry in the operations, the way I read it, at one point in time there were about 70 prisoners inside the hangar and it wasn't until later on that the number of prisoners rose to about 180. If you add the two figures up, that would seem to be the result.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thereabouts, Mr. Vasic. 181, possibly 182. Certainly about 180 people, roughly speaking, inside the hangar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My learned friend asked you some questions about the military police unit. You told him that the military police company belonging to the 80th Brigade was there guarding the prisoners, but I think the true issue behind that question was a different one. However, my colleague dropped that line of questions. That's on page 59. I'm going to ask you: In addition to this military police company of the 80th Brigade, which was certainly guarding the prisoners and that's beyond dispute so I'm not going into that, was there any other military police unit in the hangar or near the hangar on the evening of the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, for a military police unit to be there for any reason whatsoever, throughout the night, with the exception of the military police company from the 80th Motorised Brigade, it was not necessary and there was none. There was a group of military police officers that came by during the night to ask if there were any problems. They stayed briefly and they were off. As for those who were escorting the POWs I'm certain that some policemen were involved but they only stayed for as long as they needed to take charge of the prisoners and they were off on a different mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said there were some policemen there who stayed briefly and were off. Which unit did those people belong to?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember, Mr. Vasic. It's really beyond me to remember whether that was the military police company belonging to the Guards Brigade or a different military police unit, but I really can't -- believe me, I can't remember. I can't for the life of me remember, as -- try as I might, and I really don't wish to be speculating about something I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But that was not the military police unit that belonged to your unit, the military police company belonging to your unit.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ours were busy securing a site elsewhere. And they were all the military police that I had, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it might be a convenient time for our first break. It's 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes to 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Danilovic, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we please have Exhibit 426. This is something that you were cross-examined on by my learned friend, Mr. Moore. This is a combat report produced by the command of OG South dated the 23rd of November at 1800 hours. First of all, sir, when a daily combat report is produced, what does it cover? What time period does it cover?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, it covers the time elapsed between the previous combat report and the new one, which is normally a 24-hour period, unless one is dealing with an interim combat report, which is also sometimes submitted to a superior command if a combat situation so requires.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What we see in front of us -- well, you can see for yourself, it's a combat report dated the 23rd of November, 1991, 1800 hours. This is a regular or daily combat report. Which specific period does this one cover, sir, in terms of the time-line specified.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It covers the period between 1800 hours on the 22nd and 1800 hours on the 23rd of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's leave this report aside for the time being. Could we please have Exhibit 425, now. That is the previous combat report dated the 22nd of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we please zoom in on the last two paragraphs. Sir, can you look at the last paragraph and tell me: Before this combat report was produced the time being as specified here, were all the documents, all the control and command documents within the zone of the operations group handed over to the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those documents that were necessary in order to exercise control and command of the units were handed over, and that is what the daily combat report indicates.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we please have Exhibit 444 now. Mr. Danilovic, this is an order by the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade regulating the establishment of military authorities and the date is the 22nd of November, isn't that what it says?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the document shows. No question about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at item 7 and tell me, from the 22nd of November, 1991, the 80th Motorised Brigade continued to be subordinated to OG South?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The necessary clearing of the battleground will be organised by OG South in cooperation with the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade - so it would appear not - and in cooperation with the TO Staff, which means that at this point in time the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade is no longer subordinated to the command of OG South, nor is the TO Vukovar staff, for that matter. That is not a moot point at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will no longer be requiring this exhibit. I would like to go back to Exhibit 367 now that's the LAD PVO order, or rather the PVO order which is something that my learned friend examined you on. Can we please zoom in on the letterhead. Mr. Danilovic, you explained this to us, but perhaps we could go through this again. It's about what this order means. First of all, what do we see in the upper right hand corner, it says military secret, submit with order attachment number, copy number.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well you see this is something I didn't notice yesterday and I think I might have been a little confused by Mr. Moore, because sometimes he can ask unpleasant questions. But he is perfectly within his rights, I understand that. I see what it says here, now. It says: "Submit with order." This is something that is sent to the command of the LAD PVO and it comes from the command of OG South. This is the first copy, copy number 2; copy number 1 stays with OG South, with the command, and copy number 2 goes to the anti-aircraft protection unit in its zone of responsibility, in the zone of responsibility of the subordinate unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This order for an attack as an ongoing mission, is this sent by the command of OG South to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic, by all means. This is enshrined in the rules. Everyone knows that the directly superior command is required to submit an order in writing for any mission, for any combat activity, be it attack, or defence. In any case, there must be a combat order, with attachments, depending on what the focus is on. Maybe some attachments, maybe all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about these attachments that are enclosed in a combat order as an ongoing mission, is this also forwarded to the branches and services of the command of a subordinate unit, the 80th Motorised Brigade in this specific case?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these attachments are submitted, they normally are, especially if there is sufficient time to carry out a combat mission. If time is short, then only those attachments tend to be submitted that are essential for the implementation of a specific combat mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about ongoing combat assignments, Mr. Danilovic, those that apply throughout, the totality of combat operations. When an order is received from a superior command, OG South, for example, to a command like the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade, and when there are attachments arriving with it in relation to certain branches and services, are these attachments submitted to the chiefs of the respective branches and services within the command of, for example, the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. The PVO chief, since we're talking about the 80th LAD PVO, receives this order from his directly superior command. He's then required to draft a PVO order and submit this order to the commander of the 80th LAD PVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In order to carry out an order like this, stemming from a number of ongoing assignments issued to the command of a subordinate unit - in our example, the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade - who is it that submits reports to the superior command, in this case the command of OG South?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the brigade command that submits these reports. A joint report for all branches and services involved. This is done by the brigade command. It's not as if there are individual lines of reporting, the PVO chief, the chief of engineers, and so on and so forth. A joint report is produced. Only there is a need for an interim report to be written and sent is anything done differently. Then you have an interim report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you look at this PVO order, the one that we see in front of us, did these reports go through the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade to the command of OG South?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the 80th Motorised Brigade submitted a regular daily combat report, with references to PVO-relate the issues within the framework of other missions that were carried out. Therefore a joint report is drawn up as opposed to individual reports being sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Between the 9th of November, 1991 and the 22nd of November, 1991 under whose command was the LAD PVO of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state with sure and certain knowledge that in its entirety it was throughout under the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade, or rather under the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, and it was for that purpose that they carried out special tasks. I can't be positive that never at any time any of its batteries were not attached to another unit for a specific mission. I can't state that in no uncertain terms. Any attachments were brief, if any. But the LAD PVO operated under the command of the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say that the LAD PVO operated under the command of the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade. Was it part of the framework of the general Vukovar area PVO, as some sort of an umbrella institution?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at this order by OG South, you will see that there are detailed descriptions of missions for all the units within the zone of responsibility of OG South, and I don't think that there is any question about that. If there's anything that strikes you as unusual, I'm at your service, and I will gladly explain everything that I can help you with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Danilovic. You were shown by my learned friend, Mr. Moore, Exhibit 375 which is the war log of the 80th Motorised Brigade. I'm sure you will remember that yesterday Mr. Moore asked you about various entries to the war log in connection with the LAD PVO division, that's pages 66 through 71 on the unofficial transcript. He went from date to date and asked you to read the entries. It says, "the LAD PVO is working according to the plan of operations of OG South." You explained what that means. At one point he asked you specifically about the 13th of November, and we could please have that pulled up on our screens, that's Exhibit 375, and the date is the 13th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the operations log or the war log?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It's the war log. This is Exhibit 375. It's the entry dated 13th of November, 1800 hours, and Mr. Moore asked you to read out the part about LAD PVO which says that it was under the command of OG South. You explained yesterday that this was a mistake, and that this was entered erroneously. I will not ask you about the 13th, but about the 14th. The following day. The 14th of November, 1800 hours. Please find the entry saying something about LAD PVO.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean 1700? Or 1800?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that it reads 1800, although it is in small script. But it is certainly the 14th of November of 1991.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have here is -- reads 1700 and then 17 hours, 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the war log. You are looking at the operations log.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is certainly the war log. Here, under the 14th of November, it says: So far the regular combat reports received from, and then a list of units follows. LAD PVO, HAD, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Look at the screen, whether this is the document you are reading. I mean this document, it looks like this.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the war log.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please look at the entry dated 14th of November. This page begins with the entry Negoslavci village, the 14th of November, 1800 hours. And it reads: "The 1st Motorised Battalion is still engaged," et cetera. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you sure you're not looking at the wrong document? Can we please -- can we get the B/C/S version. You are looking at the operations log. Look at the screen. Can you see the entry dated 14th of November?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the entry about LAD PVO. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: LAD PVO is still on the same positions and is operating under the tasks received from OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is it the same as the entries dated 12th of November, 13th of November, what you read out yesterday to my learned friend, Mr. Moore? So my question is, is this entry, as you have read it out, identical for all dates in this log, except for the 13th of November, 1991, of which you said yesterday that it was a mistake?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's almost the same. They're saying that they are operating according to plan, and the operation -- operational task of OG South. I don't know what kind of operations officers kept this log. This is obviously a mistake. I mentioned yesterday that there was no concrete reason. And let me give you one more example. Every day, when the commanders of battalions came for -- to the briefings, the commander of LAD PVO also came and I remember that. And this, if LAD PVO is subordinated to OG South, it would be logical for them to go there for their briefings and they were coming to the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to this evidence. It's, again, speculation. Phrases like "it's obvious," "this is obviously a mistake." And I would submit that the witness himself has no personal knowledge at all about this entry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, that point you have made and sought to make in submission and cross-examination, I would not at this point think we should interfere with Mr. Vasic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- going over once again your ground. Carry on, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Danilovic have you found the war log? Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let us now have a look at the entry dated 16th of November, 1991 and while we're waiting for this to be put on the screen, let me ask you whether this phrase that you have read out to us is operating according to the plans and the war tasks of OG South. Does that mean that LAD PVO is under the command of OG South? Or does it mean something else altogether?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, this means that LAD PVO carries out tasks according to the orders of the commander of PVO of OG South that we were receiving, and I think that's the way it was. It can't be any -- anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And who was in command of the PVO of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now, let's go to Exhibit number 375, the date is 16th of November. Can you read this out to us.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you don't have it in front of you, look at the screen. The entry into the war log dated 16th of November, 1800 hours. Please find the item referring to LAD PVO.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it after NPOAD [as interpreted]. LAD PVO, was engaged in anti-aircraft security from the existing area. The third battery of LAD PVO was attacked at 1400 hours and at 0200 hours. Fire was opened in return in return. No losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you please look, who is submitting this report?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is submitted to the commander of the LAD PVO, as did all the commanders of the battalions that were part of the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Apart from this statement in the war log, does it say any where who was submitting the report?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here on the right, you can see that it is Captain First Class Marcek.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now return to the operations log which is Exhibit 371. So let us, please, have a look at the entry dated 18th of November -- 17th of November. 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you have found it, then we can put the English version on the screen. So the 17th of November, 1800 hours, this is now the operations log. I will read it out. "The commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade has decided. Extended the operations of the third motorised battalion. Break through to the Vuka river and prevent the enemy from withdrawing from the northern part of the town of Vukovar. Through the engagement of the HAD and the LAD PVO, support the breaking up of enemy forces in the northern part of Vukovar, establishing the most favourable conditions for the final liberation of Vukovar." Mr. Danilovic, does this entry include an order referring to the LAD PVO of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Vasic. Can you repeat the exact hour and date? I have problems here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: 17th of November, 1800 hours. This is the operations log. So the 17th of November at 1800 hours. If you cannot find it --

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it. This says LAD PVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So this is an order to LAD PVO?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operation, through the engagement of the HAD and LAD PVO, support the breaking up of enemy forces in the northern part of Vukovar. And then it says: "Establishing the most favourable conditions." So it is obvious that the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade gives out an order to the commander of the LAD PVO. So that commander will have been under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And what kind of order is he giving out?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: To support the breaking up of enemy forces in the northern part of Vukovar, so to provide artillery support to the units operating in the northern part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade be able to give an order to the commander of the LAD PVO, if that unit had been resubordinated to OG South?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, the practice was, and this is really what it was, that LAD PVO, if they really had been resubordinated to OG South, then the order would have had to come from the command of OG South, and that's really how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. All right. Let's continue. My learned friend, Mr. Moore, asked you a number of questions referring to a hypothetical situation about the reports related to the command -- the town command. If a group of officers or at a certain time units that would have to report to the commander of a certain zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic. That is mandatory, if a group of officers, individuals come to the zone of responsibility of another unit, they should report to the highest ranking officer there and explain the reasons for their presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And if it should happen that that officer does not report and the town commander receives information of officers or a unit present in his zone of responsibility, does the town commander have to approach those officers or units and ask them about the reasons for their presence there?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely. The command, in that case, would have to establish contact with those officers or units to find out why they were there and then take appropriate measures. Whether the unit had arrived upon the orders of a superior unit to provide support will have to be found out by the commander of that zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If that unit were to arrive to that territory to carry out a task that had previously been -- of which the commander of the town who had previously been informed, what then?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the unit or some officer from the command of, let's say the brigade, would have to receive that unit and, in accordance with the order of the superior command, engage it, or rather employ it for the accomplishment of the mission it was sent there to accomplish.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If that task or mission had not been ordered by the superior command, what would the procedure be for the commander of the town?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
