utterances.text: It would be the following. If I were in that role, I would remove that unit from the zone of operations of my unit, and I would inform the superior command of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Danilovic, is the town commander in every -- in any case responsible for the officers or the group of officers in that territory? Does he have to inform them of the rules in force there? Is he obliged to do that under the rules in force for a barracks' duty?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town commander is responsible for the organisation of all measures and activities as stipulated by the Rules of Service, and if a unit arrived there, upon the orders of a superior command, he has to provide accommodation or deploy it, in accordance with the Rules of Service. I see no other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Based on what you have said, he is the one who deploys and employs those units, if they were sent there?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if they were sent there, upon the orders of a superior command, he will act in accordance with that order, otherwise he will remove them from his zone of responsibility and put an end to it. There is no other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Danilovic, does the entry of any unit, even a unit from a superior command, whether announced in advance or not, into the zone of responsibility of the town command relieve the commander from any responsibilities or lessen his powers in that zone, in any way?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: An arrival, announced or not, of such a unit cannot possibly mean that the responsibility of the town commander is, by any way -- is, in any way, relieved or lessened for his zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If the town commander were informed that a group of POWs would be taken to a facility in his zone of responsibility, would he have to prepare security for that group if that were his task, and get acquainted with the situation on the ground and find out when that group is scheduled to arrive there?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, the town commander, if he receives such an order, is obliged to take all preparatory measures in accordance with the Rules of Service, to inform the prison to appoint security and receive those prisoners and put them into prison. If there is -- there aren't enough soldiers for security, he must request reinforcement from the superior command to enable him to carry out his task, that is provide security for the prisoners until their evacuation into the zones, into the designated zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the rule is, I suppose, that the superior command issues orders to a subordinate -- subordinated unit, bearing in mind the capabilities of that unit. Is that a rule that is in force in the army?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, superior commanders, when issuing orders, assess whether the commander of that subordinated unit is capable of really carrying out that task. And most times tasks assigned are realistic. If they cannot be accomplished, then the unit in question is reinforced with manpower or other means, such as equipment, to enable them to carry out the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If a town commander receives resubordinated units, the task of which is to provide security, what would the town commander be obliged to do?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would have to employ those units in accordance with the order received from the superior command in order to achieve -- or accomplish his mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If one of the tasks were the guarding of POWs in that territory, whose decision would it be? Which unit should be employed for the guarding of those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the unit who is assigned such a task will have to assess -- make an assessment and decide what units and what means to use in order to safely carry out that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would that town commander, while taking that decision, have the right and the obligation to employ units that were resubordinated to him in that region?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: All subordinated units are at the disposal of the commander, and he can employ them without prior approval of the superior command, but only in accordance with rules of engagement and in accordance with the task to be carried out by that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If those units were tasked to provide security in a certain area, could these units be employed for the guarding of war prisoners in the case of need?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of need, those units would certainly be employed to guard the POWs that arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday my learned friend, Mr. Moore, asked you about a hypothetical situation in which the town commander goes to see his superior commander requesting for help. My question to you is whether that town commander is obliged to employ all the units at his disposal before asking for -- asking the superior commander for help.

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I can tell you what I personally would have done. A capable and resolved commander is obliged to carry out the received task, and in that sense employ all the units subordinated to him; that is, all the units under his command. If, for any reason, he is unable to carry out the task given to him, he is obliged to ask for instructions and help for the carrying out of that task from the superior commander. I'm saying what I would have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And if the town commander were to turn up at the superior command, without having employed any unit that were at his disposal to carry out the task of providing security in the area, what would the superior commander tell him under the rules of service?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the rules of service, the superior commander would have to give him an order to carry out the task. That's the only option.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And with regard to the forces?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: By using all the forces that are under his command that were resubordinated to him, and if that is not enough he should request additional forces from his superior commander. There is no other option.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And here is my last question. Is it common military practice for an officer to request help from a superior command without having employed all the resources at his disposal in his own units?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I can tell you from personal experience that such instances are rare. It is mostly incapable commanders who would do so without having used or having employed all units at their disposal. That was a case in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was your commander, Mr. Vojnovic, an incapable commander?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say for certain that Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic was highly capable commander, and that he was among the first officers to enter Vukovar. That was -- that's what my fellow officers and soldiers were telling me while I was -- when I returned from my mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now the last point. Mr. Moore asked you about -- asked you about what you knew about the events at Ovcara, and you explained the situation several times over. Let me only ask you: Bearing in mind what you said yourself, that the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade should have taken measures if there was a reason for measures to be taken, did you believe the stories that you had heard from people? Did you believe them, although these things were never mentioned at the official meetings of the 80th -- the command of the 80th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADE DANILOVIC:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody informed me, from the command or the staff, about that event, so that I took no measures to that effect. And I had -- I had many other things that gave me a headache, such as the identification of dead bodies, the team of pathologists, they were receiving about 400 dead bodies per day, whether it was at the brick factory or elsewhere. What was important to me was the information that the crime had been committed by the TO. But I was not responsible for them. They were not subordinated to me. And I -- at that moment I did not pay attention to that, because I had other things that gave me a headache.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Danilovic. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Danilovic, you will be pleased to know that that completes your questioning. We would thank you for your attendance here and the assistance that you have given the Chamber, and you are now free to return to your other interests. Thank you, indeed. The Court officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Parker, I thank you too. And one thing I would like to ask you, you promised the other day that I would be given a chance to greet Mr. Sljivancanin and Mr. Radic, Judge Borovic. I can't see General Mrksic. We only met once, by your leave, Your Honours I can't afford to be adamant but I would really like to exchange greetings with them. They were my fellow soldiers and we went through difficult times together. I am shaken by everything that this trial is about. I am shaken by everything that we, as former JNA officers, had to experience and survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It may be possible for you to find an opportunity when we rise to meet them, and you can ask the victims' unit whether that can be arranged. We must now go on to deal with some other matters. You will understand that that precludes us just allowing you a social opportunity here at this moment. So I thank you. If you would go with the Court officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasic, are you in a position, first, to indicate the latest bulletin on your client's health?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please perhaps discuss this in private session. The news I have is somewhat complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm sorry. I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It was my fault for out staying my welcome in private session, so to speak, but there were all these issues to be dealt with. I would now like to ask Mr. Domazet to tell us about the position regarding these remaining witnesses, with all the different circumstances that affect the course of action to be taken. Some of them are real and some of them have been subpoenaed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first and foremost, I will try to explain the situation in relation to P-019. My travel over the weekend was approved and I went to Zagreb to speak to this witness in a bid to convince him to appear and testify before this court. As I told you last week, the first time I spoke to that witness was on Wednesday. This was a successful conversation. We hit it off rather well. We talked about a great many things, including his present job. He thought it was a good idea to meet and discuss everything, and he said that either Saturday or Sunday might be the most convenient for him since he spends most work days out in the field on business. That was why I requested authorisation to travel, which I obtained. Just before I set out, I called witness P-019 again to announce my arrival and now the situation was quite different. His condition had obviously changed. He told me he might be in hospital and that it wasn't a good idea for me to travel, because he probably couldn't see me. I told him I had to go, because I'd bought the ticket already and my request had been approved. If he was still in hospital, well that was something that I would have to live with. Upon my arrival in Zagreb, on Sunday morning I arrived outside his house. I saw his name on the bell. I rang. His wife replied. When I asked about him, she said that he was out walking with their children, with their daughters, and that she had no idea when he would be back. She refused to open the door. Therefore, I did not actually meet her. I said that I would drop by again later, which I did. I then took the opportunity to go back to my hotel and phone her, since I didn't want to use the intercom to discuss any details, any passersby would have been able to overhear our conversation. When I phoned her, she told me her husband was still not back from the walk. I talked to her and tried to convince her that it was necessary for me to meet her husband and that she could attend our meeting too, if she wanted to. I said all I wanted to talk to him about was his possible testimony, or to see if he had, in the meantime decided otherwise. She promised this would be possible in the afternoon, and she told me to call back in the afternoon. However, what had happened that morning -- and this is something that I only found out after I returned from Zagreb, and this was shocking to me -- she obviously took down the registration plate number of the car in which I was driven there and I was driven there by the son of one of my late friends from Zagreb, whom I had asked to later take me to the grave, this friend of mine who was his father who happened to be a close friend who died two months ago. So the son just waited in the car for me to have this conversation. He had no idea who I would speak to, or what about. She obviously submitted this phone number to the police, the registration plate, the registration number of the car, and the police sought him out at work and he happens to be one of the directors in the company where he is employed, to interview him and to find out who he had been spending time with the previous weekend. I only found out when I was back from Zagreb. Then this afternoon I called the witness at his flat again. His wife picked up the phone. She said he was asleep, and was not willing to talk to me. She said there was nothing for us to talk about and there must be some sort of hidden agenda involved. I told her again about what my mission was and what I wanted to achieve. I was under the impression at one time that I had managed to convince her, and she said once her husband woke up, he would give me a call. I gave her my hotel room number. I said I would be at the hotel and I said that they could set both the time and place for our appointment. However, when I tried calling back, by using their home number, there was no response at all. No one picked up the phone. To me it now seemed quite obvious that the witness was anxious to avoid meeting me and to avoid this appointment which he had previously agreed to. His wife said that he would be going to the District Court in Zagreb the next Monday, because he had received a summons and that he would explain everything to them. Based on what we received yesterday afternoon, I realised that he did indeed go to the district court in Zagreb yesterday and he did receive a summons. He was officially served his subpoena, which he subsequently signed but there is nothing to indicate his reaction. There is nothing to indicate whether he agreed or refused. None of the boxes were filled. He didn't say whether he would eventually appear before the ICTY or not. A little later there is another letter that we received. There had been phone communication to the effect that he had been hospitalised and that medical documents would be forthcoming. That is about as much as I know in relation to this witness. We are still in the dark as to whether he has accepted to come and testify or whether his is a final refusal. There is also the possibility that he is undergoing treatment. We might be receiving documents to that effect. That is the story of the week I spent in Zagreb and, as you see, I was entirely unable to meet this witness, despite my best efforts. I hardly have anything to add about that. The Mrksic Defence stands by its formal application to have this witness heard in court. He has not ruled it out or that's at least how it appears to be. Given the fact that he is now in hospital he can hardly do anything about it, if the whole story is true. It goes without saying. But the way things happened over the weekend with his wife and him, being obviously very anxious to avoid meeting me, and obviously being in an eager mood to kick up a fuss and create some problems over this man who drove me there, is indication enough of their intentions. As for Jovica Puskar, we have received a certificate from the cardiology department of the military medical academy in Belgrade. There was an emergency and he was admitted and treated. As Mr. Vasic said, given his condition, he's quite obviously unable to travel to The Hague and appear as a witness. We shall be filing a motion in the course of the day containing these documents and we shall be filing an application for this witness to be heard via videolink, especially in view of the fact that this will not be a lengthy witness. Then there is the last witness who has been subpoenaed, witness Gluscevic. The subpoena was served on him. He is now back in Belgrade, but managed to get in touch. After talking to me he agreed to come and testify. Therefore, he did not decide to disobey the subpoena, although, for personal, family and health reasons -- and this is especially something that concerns his wife -- he would prefer to testify via videolink, from Belgrade, and perhaps this could be arranged on the same day that Jovica Puskar testifies, with the Chamber's approval, of course. We must take into account the fact that this is another witness who should address a number of really crucial issues. This notwithstanding, the examination will not be a lengthy one and we believe it will be perfectly possible to do the whole thing in just one day. Witness Gluscevic is not in possession of a passport, regardless of all these measures. He applied for one and he might get one today. He might get one as soon as today. So should the Chamber not agree to have him testify via videolink, there is some chance that we might ensure his arrival, certainly not before Monday. If all the conditions are in place for the trial to continue on Monday and here I am also referring to Mr. Mrksic's presence, then perhaps he might be heard; that is, of course, if the Chamber agrees and approves this motion. Unless the Chamber approves this motion for this witness to be heard via videolink, and then there is also the motion about evidence that we shall be submitting in relation to some exhibits that were not tendered through particular witnesses. This is particularly in relation to some exhibits that were supposed to be introduced through witness P-019. That's all I can say about our remaining witnesses. If any further information is needed, I will be happy to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, the motion about this documentary evidence, when is that to be filed?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for this brief consultation with Mr. Vasic. We shall try to do that as soon as possible, tomorrow at the latest, in as far as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is any other counsel wanting to put any submission? Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would not like to repeat myself or the objections that I raised yesterday in relation to all of this evidence. Those objections remain. The victims and witnesses unit has produced a plan for my witnesses, in terms of their flight tickets, hotel accommodation, their arrival in The Hague, and so on and so forth, as I have informed the Chamber. Out of respect, I would also like to inform the Court that my colleague, Mr. Weiner, kindly asked me to postpone the witness who was due to appear the following Monday, but I would prefer to leave that to the Chamber to rule upon. My position is well known as far as the reason is concerned and it is, after all, a matter of judicial economy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I merely wanted to remind the Chamber of the ruling that was made on Friday. It was said that we would discuss the exclusion of our client's statements and we wrote another motion in reply, and my understanding was the OTP were supposed to respond to that by yesterday, but we received nothing since last Monday. We certainly would like to see a ruling by the Trial Chamber as soon as possible, since Mr. Radic is due to start his testimony. I think it might be material to all of us in the courtroom to know what the Chamber's position is on the use of our client's statements in cross-examination. It was my intention to discuss this orally, but the gentleman wanted to have everything in writing, so that's what we did. What I said yesterday is nothing new, in terms of fresh arguments. It is just further clarification on our part following the OTP response. I believe that you are now fully in the picture, as it were, and that you are now in a position to make your final ruling. And the OTP should be clear about the position, too. The other issue that I was going to raise today was the OTP and their arguments for continuing to oppose the MFI 576, Goran Hadzic interview to be tendered into evidence. I was told that there would be brief oral arguments about this, but he's not around, so I don't know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we need, I believe, to deal firstly with the question of Mr. Mrksic's evidence, and then look at what else might need attention, except to say that as soon as we have the written submissions we hope speedily to give you the decision in respect of your client's interviews and it would be the Chamber's plan that you have that decision on Friday, so that it would be available for you to have guidance as evidence is led from Mr. Borovic's client and then yours, in due course. Is there anything, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, there is. Whether in actual fact it should be dealt with now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Only in respect of the question of future evidence of Mr. Mrksic, and the closing of his case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With regard to Mr. Mrksic's submissions, we have no submission. I was asked by my learned friend whether we would object if they reserved their position in relation to witnesses because of medical difficulty, and we would have no objection to that, of course. In relation to any other matter, in respect of Mr. Mrksic, I have no submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what you're saying, there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Very simply this. If there are medical problems, which may eventually resolve themselves, and I'm talking about 019. If in actual fact 019 is released from hospital and is able to give evidence, in our submission, even though it is not for us to submit in relation to it, we would have no objection if he was to be called later in the trial, as long as the Court is satisfied that he is giving relevant and appropriate evidence. So that would be our position. We would have no objection and would not oppose that course. So if they were to reserve their position in relation to closing the case, subject to those witnesses, we would have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I hope that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to respond to this. We see what difficulty was faced by the Mrksic Defence. We opposed this motion to have witness Puskar heard later, but it is as a matter of principle that we oppose the idea to have witnesses heard once the Mrksic case has been concluded. This only applies to cases where it was possible to have the witnesses brought over during the Mrksic case, so we do not think that witness P-019 or Mr. Gluscevic should be heard once the other Defence cases are already well underway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber has indicated, in its recent decision given orally, that the Defence of Mr. Mrksic has not been able to persuade it that either witness P-019, nor the potential witness, Mr. Gluscevic, had been demonstrated to be of such importance to the conduct of this case that it was necessary and appropriate in the interests of justice for this Chamber to take whatever steps are open to it to try and ensure the attendance of either of those witnesses. That position remains unchanged. It is apparent, from what has occurred, since the rather late approach it would appear by the Defence of Mr. Mrksic to each of those two witnesses and the late attempts by subpoena to encourage their attendance, that neither witness was a ready, willing and cooperative witness. What Mr. Domazet has put to us today reinforces that with respect to witness P-019. And as he himself has indicated, the appearances are quite clear that the witness is avoiding the representatives of Mr. Mrksic's Defence, and is doing what he can to avoid attendance here. With the witness, Mr. Gluscevic, it may be, from what Mr. Domazet has said, that there could be some change in that person's attitude to cooperating with the Mrksic Defence and attending. There is the third witness, Mr. Puskar, who was approached at an earlier time and from all we know has been a willing and cooperative witness, but who has been undergoing some prolonged health problem, a problem which at the moment continues. Now, these three witnesses differ, in that the evidence which Mr. Puskar might give has been more readily identified and is limited in nature. The evidence which the other two may give, in particular perhaps that of Mr. P-019, appears conjectural and merely an attempt to indicate the sort of matters about which the witness ought to be able to speak, rather than any capacity on the part of the Mrksic Defence to indicate the specific facts about which the witness will testify. That, of course, reflects the fact that neither Mr. Gluscevic nor witness P-019 has been prepared to this point to cooperate with the Mrksic Defence, and make appropriate statements available. Against that background, the Chamber must consider whether now the time has come to bring to an end the Mrksic Defence. We have a concern to ensure that there is a proper opportunity for the presentation of that Defence. We also have a responsibility to ensure, in the interests of the other accused and all concerned and those waiting for trial, that this particular trial proceeds with all expedition that can be properly ensured, consistent with the interests of justice. Having regard to those matters, the Chamber is not persuaded that it should allow further time for attempts to ensure the attendance here of witness P-019, nor Mr. Gluscevic, subject to one matter, which I will mention shortly. I can say, with respect to Mr. Puskar, we do not presently have a motion, and we would take the view that the case for Mr. Mrksic should be brought to an end subject to there being leave given to the Mrksic Defence to bring a submission -- a motion at a later time, should Mr. Puskar's health improve, a motion that would need, then, to seek leave to re-open the Mrksic Defence and would need to demonstrate what it is was important about Mr. Puskar's evidence for that Defence, and to demonstrate, clearly, the health problems that had prevented his earlier attendance. Subject to that, the Chamber feels that it is necessary to say that the Mrksic Defence has had adequate opportunity to secure its witnesses and to secure their attendance here. We take account of and recognise the force of the submissions of the other two accused, that it would not be fair to their cases to allow a body of evidence, such as that which might fall from witness P-019 and also Mr. Gluscevic, to be led at some unforeseeable time in the future during the course of their cases, or even after their case. So with the exception, which I will mention very shortly, in the Chamber's view, the Mrksic Defence should close this week. The one qualification we put on it, given that we are told that Mr. Gluscevic might be cooperative, and that his evidence would be short and less than a day, we would take the view that if the Mrksic Defence is able to secure the attendance of that witness either Friday or Monday of next week, we would be prepared to hear his evidence and would expect his evidence to take half a day, and no more; that is his evidence and cross-examination. When I say "secure attendance" that could include evidence by videolink, if that is able to be arranged. But given the time, that may be even more difficult than securing the personal attendance of the witness. So it boils down to this, Mr. Vasic. If you can get Mr. Gluscevic here to give evidence Friday or Monday morning, or can arrange a videolink for that purpose, we will hear him for half a day. So it will have to be straight to the point. If you are not able to secure his attendance on Friday or Monday, on that basis, that would be the end of any concession we would make in respect of that witness. I think it is Monday afternoon, and not morning, I'm reminded on each side of me. So you have an extra half day to make arrangements. Otherwise, no further action by the Chamber in respect of witnesses P-019 and Mr. Gluscevic, and we would take the step that the Defence of Mr. Mrksic should formally close to allow Mr. Borovic to commence his case on Monday, as planned, except that he could be half a day late on Monday, if there proves possible for the witness, Gluscevic, to be here. We hope that half a day isn't too great a disturbance in your arrangements. And it is a matter that leave is granted to the Mrksic Defence in respect of Mr. Puskar, if at some later time it is possible for him to attend and you are able to demonstrate to us that leave should be given to you to reopen your case to hear Mr. Puskar. Now, we've run to the end of the tape. Are there other matters that need to be dealt with? I think it may be necessary to come back after the break, unless they can be dealt with in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I deal with -- there are two matters. May I deal with one and then Mr. Weiner will be able to deal with the other, because of the seating problems. I would like the Court's guidance, if I may, in relation to a matter that has arisen between my learned friend Mr. Borovic and myself. It is not a problem in the sense that there is any difficulty. It's to do with the handwriting of the document for 002. My learned friend has an expert, clearly would wish that document to be seen, but that would be in Belgrade. There are difficulties, if an expert is to be obtained by the Prosecution for clearly those two experts to liaise. I have suggested to my learned friend, Mr. Borovic, a position that arose in the case of Oric, and I believe I am correct when I say this is what occurred. That the Court ordered, through the registry, that an independent expert be found; that expert to look at the document, to operate on guidelines in relation to Prosecution/Defence, and in that case, then, if there is any handwriting analysis which may become relevant to the issue, that witness can be called. I can just foresee difficulties moving a document either to Belgrade, or Paris, or London. In my submission it would be better if it was just held here and dealt with by one expert. So I would seek the Court's guidance on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We had an agreement, Mr. Moore and I, to appoint one expert each, one expert for the Defence and another for the Prosecution. That was done by The Hague's bureau in Belgrade. Then a sample of the handwriting would be taken and a joint analysis would be made. I learned from Mr. Moore that there was a problem with an expert who he could not find, and he asked me whether I had anything against him employing an expert from Croatia. I replied, no, of course not. As far as I'm concerned, Ireland is fine also. So as for the Defence counsel, we consider that it is -- that any expert for -- handwriting expert is acceptable to us. So whatever the Chamber decides to do, whether it is one expert appointed by the Court, fine. If there are two experts, one appointed by the Defence, another by the Prosecution, who will analyse the handwriting together, that's acceptable for us too. Only I would think that we should go about this fast, but of course there should be a reason for us to verify a text in this manner. With regard to what the witness says and if there is a contradiction to what a written entry says, that is, then, a valid reason to do so. And in the interest of justice, I believe that this witness, who would be brought in as the last witness, should be asked to explain or clarify that document. We shouldn't proceed not only along three points as the Prosecution has moved, but that we should analyse the entire document, and thus undertake all of these activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well I take it, Mr. Borovic, from what you say, that if one -- one expert could be identified, it would be satisfactory for your Defence purposes for that one expert to do the work instead of two separate ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as regards the position of the Defence of Miroslav Radic, that would be satisfactory. And I would, then, make a proposal as to what should be examined. I would have to consult the other parties, but of course without delaying any -- delaying the process. So in brief, my answer is "yes".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does this bear upon either of the other accused? I think not. We would ask Mr. Moore or Mr. Borovic -- oh, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would only say that, that there is a joint proposal here by Mr. Borovic and Mr. Moore, and I support the course of action to appoint only one expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although Mr. Borovic doesn't seem to agree with me lately, but I agree with his proposal. So I'm for the appointing of one expert who will analyse the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure, with goodwill on one hand, Mr. Vasic, you will find it will be restored on both hands, yes. The Chamber would ask Mr. Borovic and Mr. Moore, if necessary in consultation with the other two Defence teams, to see if they can identify an expert, the subject matter and the location for examination, and they might perhaps come with a joint agreed motion, short and simple, and we can take the matter forward from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moore --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I understand, but could I ask the Court perhaps to order -- suggest that the Registry locate an expert. That way, then, it resolves difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That seems a sensible idea, Mr. Moore. And I can do even better: The two of you are authorised to approach the Registry on behalf of the Chamber, because the Chamber would like to get something presented which everybody is happy with, rather than have to go through each item and debate it. Now, Mr. Lukic, you need to raise something further? Am I right? I'm thinking about adjourning and resuming after the break, you see. Unless you have only got half a minute, there isn't time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will need more than 30 seconds. So if Mr. Moore agrees, we can continue after the break, or we can do so on another day. So it has to do with the interview with Goran Hadzic. In fact I would like to hear the ruling in the Krajisnik case, which is expected in a few minutes, but we can also continue our argument after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The matter will be considered briefly on Monday morning -- Monday afternoon, at 2.15. And hopefully it should take no longer than five minutes. I'm getting worried from Mr. Borovic, you see. We will now adjourn until Monday, in the afternoon, at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 2nd day of October, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: [The accused Sljivancanin and Radic enter court]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.45 p.m.,
